title: American everyday life remains structurally car-dependent while roads allocate access, work, social life, and freight through different layers
source_unit: Federal Highway Administration, Our Nation's Highways 2026: Travel, published July 31, 2026
geography: United States; public roads, National Household Travel Survey trips, vehicle miles, and domestic freight

denominator.unit: share of passenger travel trips in the National Household Travel Survey

motor_vehicle_trips.unit: percent of passenger trips using motor vehicles

car.unit: percent of passenger trips by car

suv.unit: percent of passenger trips by SUV

pickup.unit: percent of passenger trips by pickup truck

walking_biking.unit: percent of passenger trips by walking or bicycle

mobility_dependency.value: work, errands, and social activity are carried through a transportation system in which motor vehicles account for the large majority of trips

observations.method: FHWA presentation of 2022 National Household Travel Survey trip shares by travel mode.
observations.uncertainty: Trip shares do not measure trip distance, household vehicle ownership, cost, safety, accessibility, transit quality, or whether the mode was chosen or forced by place and infrastructure.
observations.subgroup: People making passenger trips in the United States, including commuting, family/personal, social/recreational, and school/church trips.
observations.counterinterpretation: Motor-vehicle dominance can reflect convenience, geography, dispersed destinations, weather, family logistics, disability access, or freight-supporting land use rather than a single cultural preference for cars.

denominator.unit: U.S. residents used in FHWA per-person travel calculation

public_road_vmt.unit: vehicle-miles traveled on public roads in the 50 states and D.C.

system_scale.value: mobility is a large recurring household, infrastructure, energy, and economic exposure rather than a marginal service category

observations.method: FHWA Highway Statistics and population-based calculations reported in Our Nation's Highways 2026.
observations.uncertainty: National mileage totals do not show distribution by income, geography, disability, race, age, vehicle ownership, trip purpose, or the household cost and time required to produce the travel.
observations.subgroup: Residents and users of public roads in the 50 states and D.C.
observations.counterinterpretation: High travel volume can reflect economic activity and access as well as burden; vehicle miles are not equivalent to welfare, productive output, or necessary travel.

observations.period: 2022; trip purpose and weekly time structure

denominator.unit: privately operated vehicle and passenger-trip shares in the National Household Travel Survey

weekday_commuting.unit: percent of weekday privately operated vehicle trips classified as commuting

weekday_family_personal.unit: percent of weekday privately operated vehicle trips for family and personal reasons, including shopping and medical appointments

weekday_social_recreation.unit: percent of weekday privately operated vehicle trips for social and recreational reasons

weekend_social_recreation.unit: percent of weekend trips for social and recreational reasons

weekend_family_personal.unit: percent of weekend trips for family and personal reasons

life_routine_route.value: the same mobility system organizes paid work, care and errands, and social/recreational participation across different parts of the week

observations.method: FHWA presentation of 2022 National Household Travel Survey trip purposes and start-time patterns for weekdays and weekends.
observations.uncertainty: Purpose categories are descriptive and do not quantify trip duration, cost, failed trips, accessibility, household substitution, or whether a trip could have been made by another mode.
observations.subgroup: People making weekday and weekend trips in the United States.
observations.counterinterpretation: A trip-purpose share does not establish that roads caused social participation or that car travel is the only route; it describes how travel demand is currently organized.

denominator.unit: U.S. public-road functional classes and domestic freight movement

arterial_road_share.unit: percent of road miles classified as arterials

arterial_vmt_share.unit: percent of vehicle miles traveled on arterials

local_road_share.unit: percent of road miles classified as local roads

local_vmt_share.unit: percent of vehicle miles traveled on local roads

truck_freight_weight.unit: percent of domestic freight moved by weight via truck in 2023

access_mobility_split.value: arterials carry disproportionate mobility while local roads provide disproportionate access, creating a built-in tradeoff between movement and proximity

observations.method: FHWA functional-class road-mile and VMT shares plus Freight Analysis Framework 5.5.1 domestic freight measures.
observations.uncertainty: Functional class does not measure actual sidewalk, transit, safety, congestion, maintenance, or neighborhood access; freight weight is not freight value, ton-miles, or household price impact.
observations.subgroup: Road users, local communities, freight-dependent firms, and households receiving goods and services through the public-road network.
observations.counterinterpretation: The mobility/access split can support efficient movement and local access simultaneously in some places; it does not by itself establish that road design produces inequality or a particular household outcome.

related_sources.claim: The National Household Travel Survey is the underlying federal travel-behavior source cited for passenger-trip mode and purpose measures.
FHWA's Our Nation's Highways 2026 collection provides the broader roads, travel, safety, and freight chapters surrounding the travel page.

boundary: This record adds a mobility-dependency layer: motor vehicles dominate passenger trips, travel volume is enormous, work/family/social routines are organized through the road system, arterials carry disproportionate VMT, local roads provide disproportionate access, and trucking carries most domestic freight by weight. It does not estimate household transport cost, emissions, safety, accessibility, inequality, or causal effects of road design.
